returns 1 when the game should get the touch. |\n| `NitroPort_LowerMenuTakePress` / `PressPending` / `PressDouble` | 0032/0036 | The press queue (30-frame lifetime), double-tap flag. |\n| `NitroPort_LowerMenuButtonAt(x,y)` / `PanelAt(x,y,&dsX,&dsY)` | always | Hit tests. |\n| `NitroPort_LowerMenuSetPanel(shows)` / `Panel()` | 0033 | What the panel shows: `PANEL_DS` or `PANEL_MAP`. |\n| `NitroPort_LowerMenuFadePanel(black)` / `PanelFade()` / `SetClock(now)` / `PanelShown(stamp)` / `FadeToPanel(shows)` | 0036 | The panel's fade to black and back (8 frames, `NITRO_LOWERMENU_FADE_FRAMES`). |\n| `NitroPort_LowerMenuKeepShown(on)` / `KeptShown()` | 0036/0037 | The menu stays drawn while the game swaps what's under it. |\n| `NitroPort_LowerMenuSetPanelRuns(runs,count)` / `PanelRuns` / `PanelShowsUpper` / `RunRow` | 0038 | The canvas assembled from runs of rows (lower screen / upper screen / tabs). |\n| `NitroPort_LowerMenuSetTabs(count,labels,active,style)` | 0038 | The port-drawn folder tabs. |\n| `NitroPort_LowerMenuSetPanelButtons(rects,count)` / `PanelButtonHeld` | 0039 | Up to 32 rectangles in canvas pixels the port takes touches on itself. |\n| `NitroPort_LowerMenuMapBegin/Sprite/Dot/Layout/Text/NoText/End/MapTextKept` | 0033/0036 | The Town Map told to the port. |\n| `NitroPort_LowerMenuMapAvailable` / `SetMap` / `SetMapWorker` / `MapWork` / `LockMap` / `TryLockMap` / `TakeMapDirtyRows` / `UnlockMap` / `MapSerial` | 0033/0036 | The map's picture and its drawer thread. |\n\n---\n\n## 3. The runtime side: `port_lowermenu.c`\n\n### 3.1 There is no single \"mode\" enum — it is a set of independent flags plus one fade state machine\n\n`port_lowermenu.c` lines 30–137 define the whole state:\n\n| Variable | Meaning |\n|---|---|\n| `sAvailable` | The platform can show the menu (set by `NitroPort_LowerMenuSetAvailable`). |\n| `sOn` | The menu is on (the game's Pokétch handlers). |\n| `sKeepShown` | The menu stays drawn while the game swaps what's under it (an app coming and going). |\n| `sTall` | The lower screen's engine is drawn 248 lines tall. |\n| `sPanelShows` | `NITRO_LOWERMENU_PANEL_DS` or `NITRO_LOWERMENU_PANEL_MAP`. |\n| `sSelected`, `sHeld`, `sEnabled`, `sFemale`, `sItems[2]` | The cursor button, the button a finger is on, the enabled bitmask, the player's gender, the two squares' items. |\n| `sRuns[]`, `sRunCount`, `sRunSerial`, `sRunsUpper` | The canvas assembled from runs (0038). |\n| `sTabCount`, `sTabActive`, `sTabLabels[4][16]`, `sTabStyle` | The port's folder tabs. |\n| `sButtons[32][4]`, `sButtonCount` | The panel's own buttons (0039/0040). |\n| `sFadeFrom`, `sFadeTo`, `sFadeStart`, `sFadeAsked`, `sFadeWaitSub`, `sPanelNext`, `sDsWait`, `sDsPop`, `sDsShown`, `sDsKnown` | The fade state machine. |\n| `sPicture[320*240]`, `sDraw[320*240]`, `sDirtyY0/sDirtyY1`, `sSerial` | The shared picture (RGBA8888, `(r<<24)\\|(g<<16)\\|(b<<8)\\|a`). |\n| `sPend`, `sPendText[2]`, `sKeptText[2][8]`, `sSub`, `sSubText[2]`, `sWork`, `sMapPic[240*232]`, `sMapPicSerial`, `sMapPicReady`, `sMapLock`, `sMapPicLock` | The map's hand-over chain. |\n\nThe **only real state machine** is the panel's fade:\n\n* `NitroPort_LowerMenuFadePanel(black)` (line 1327): `black == NITRO_LOWERMENU_CLEAR_NOW` (−1) clears at once and sets `sPanelNext = -1` (a pending tab change is called off); `black != 0` fades to black (16) via `fade_to(16, now, 0)`; `black == 0` fades back to clear, **unless** a tab change is pending (then it fades in by itself).\n* `NitroPort_LowerMenuFadeToPanel(shows)` (line 1352): remembers `sPanelNext = shows` and fades to black; the change is made later, when the panel is actually black.\n* `NitroPort_LowerMenuPanelFade()` (line 1373): called by the platform **every frame**; it completes the pending change once `fade_level(now) >= 16`, then fades back in (the DS's lower screen waits `FADE_DS_HOLD` = 4 frames for a fresh picture; the map waits until the map has been drawn as given, `FADE_WAIT_MAX` = 30 frames).\n\nThe **fade level** is a 0…16 integer (`NitroPort_LowerMenuPanelFade()` returns it); the platforms draw black over the panel by as much (REMASTER 1697–1699: \"The platforms draw black over the panel by as much (the compositor a black quad, the PC runner its pixels darkened)\").\n\n### 3.2 How a state is entered and left — the call order the game drives\n\nThe port is entirely **reactive**: the game tells it, and the platform asks it.\n\n```\n[game's thread]                          [the port]                     [the platform, every frame]\nNitroPort_LowerMenuShow(1)      ─────►   sOn = 1; redraw()  ─────►  LockFrame/TakeDirtyRows → texture\nNitroPort_LowerMenuSetEnabled(m) ───►   sEnabled = m; redraw()\nNitroPort_LowerMenuSelect(b)    ───►   sSelected = b; redraw()\nNitroPort_LowerMenuSetItem(...)  ───►   read_item_icon(); redraw()\nNitroPort_LowerMenuSetPanel(p)  ───►   sPanelShows = p; serial++\nNitroPort_LowerMenuFadePanel(1) ───►   fade_to(16,...)\nNitroPort_LowerMenuFadeToPanel(p)──►   sPanelNext = p; fade_to(16,...)\nNitroPort_LowerMenuKeepShown(1) ───►   sKeepShown = 1; redraw()\nNitroPort_LowerMenuSetPanelRuns(...)──► sRuns; serial++\nNitroPort_LowerMenuSetTabs(...)  ───►   sTab*; redraw()\nNitroPort_LowerMenuSetPanelButtons()──► sButtons\n                                      PanelFade()  ─────►  level 0..16 → black quad\n                                      LowerMenuTouch() ───►  routing + presses\n```\n\n`NitroPort_LowerMenuShow` (line 1134) is the only entry point with side effects beyond the flags: it reads the start-menu icons from the ROM on the first call (`read_icons()`, line 402 — `graphic/menu_gra.narc`, member 6 `icons_NCGR` in member 5 `menu_NCLR`), and on turning **off** it clears `sTall`, restores `sPanelTouch = 1`, drops the tabs and the panel runs/buttons, and bumps the serial so the platform stops drawing it.\n\n### 3.3 How the panel's contents are produced — **both**, but not by re-rendering the game's screens\n\nThree different producers, combined by the compositor:\n\n1. **The port's own UI** (drawn on the CPU in `port_lowermenu.c`): the frame, the button column, the eight names in a small font of the port's own (`sGlyphs`, 19 capitals 9 rows tall — \"the game's is too wide for a button, POKéDEX is 42 pixels in it\", `port_lowermenu.c` lines 5–8), the icons (six from the ROM, two drawn by hand as ASCII art: MAP and POKéTCH), the two squares and their item icons (read from `itemtool/itemdata/item_icon.narc` by `read_item_icon()`, line 629), the tabs (`draw_tabs()`, line 979). This is `draw()` (line 745) into `sDraw`, then `redraw()` (line 1053) copies `sDraw` → `sPicture` under `sLock` and bumps `sSerial`.\n2. **The DS's lower screen inside the panel**: the port does **not** re-render it. The game renders it (the Pokétch) onto the DS's sub engine; the platform's compositor takes that picture (from the 2D renderer) and draws it over the panel as **three quads** (the top row, the 192 rows, the bottom row) — REMASTER 1731–1734: \"The panel: a canvas 256 x 247 DS pixels, drawn 240 x 232 at (3, 4) … Three quads from the DS's picture's texture.\"\n3. **The map inside the panel**: a picture of its own (`sMapPic`, 240×232), drawn by `port_lowermap.c` on the map drawer thread and put over the panel the same way.\n\nFor an app whose **two** DS screens both go in the panel (the trainer case), the canvas is assembled from **runs of rows** (`NitroPort_LowerMenuSetPanelRuns`): each run is from the lower screen's rows, the upper screen's rows (at the DS's 256 columns), or the port's tabs; with a step of +1/−1/0 and optional painted side columns (`sides`, `sidesIn`).\n\n### 3.4 Key functions and their call order (port-internal)\n\n```\nNitroPort_LowerMenuShow(on)\n   └─ read_icons()                 (first time only: menu_gra.narc)\n   └─ redraw()\n        ├─ icon_from_rows()        (MAP / POKéTCH, first time)\n        ├─ draw()                  → background, panel box, button column, icons,\n        │                            names, the two squares, draw_tabs()\n        ├─ lock(); memcpy(sDraw → sPicture); sDirtyY0=0; sDirtyY1=H; sSerial++; unlock()\n\nevery frame, by the platform:\nNitroPort_LowerMenuPanelFade()     → the fade level (completes a pending tab change)\nNitroPort_LowerMenuTouch(down,x,y,&dsX,&dsY)\n   ├─ sFrames++; hand_over()       (a map waiting for the drawer's lock)\n   ├─ if (NitroPort_LowerMapFrameChanges(++sMapFrame) && map_shown()) want_map_work();\n   ├─ route the touch (sTouchIn 0..5, see §5)\n   ├─ if (held != sHeld) { sHeld = held; redraw(); }\nNitroPort_LowerMenuLockFrame(&serial) / TakeDirtyRows / UnlockFrame  → the platform uploads the picture\n```\n\n### 3.5 The map hand-over chain (the part that runs off the game's thread)\n\n```\n[game's thread]                     [the port]                         [the map drawer thread]\nMapBegin()                      →   sPend cleared\nMapSprite/MapDot/MapLayout/...  →   sPend filled (sprites, dots, hidden bit, zoom scroll)\nMapText(which,x,y,wTiles,hTiles,tiles,palette,key)\n                                 →   sPendText[which] = tiles+palette; kept in sKeptText[which][8]\nMapEnd()                         →   sPendWaiting = 1; hand_over()\n                                     hand_over(): if the drawer holds sMapLock → try next frame;\n                                     else copy sPend→sSub, sPendText→sSubText, sSubSerial++\n                                     → want_map_work() → sMapWake() (the platform's thread)\n                                                                      NitroPort_LowerMenuMapWork():\n                                                                        sWork = sSub (texts kept)\n                                                                        text_pixels()  → 4bpp tiles → RGB555 pixels\n                                                                        NitroPort_LowerMapSetFrame(sMapFrame)\n                                                                        NitroPort_LowerMapSet(&sWork)\n                                                                        publish_map() → copies the dirty rows into sMapPic\n                                                                                        and bumps sMapPicSerial\n                                                                      LockMap/TakeMapDirtyRows/UnlockMap → the platform\n```\n\nThe game never waits for the drawer: `hand_over()` returns without doing anything if the drawer holds the lock, and the next `NitroPort_LowerMenuTouch` retries (comment at `port_lowermenu.c` lines 1748–1751).\n\n### 3.6 The touch-routing state machine (`sTouchIn`)\n\n`port_lowermenu.c` lines 42–46 document it:\n\n```\n/* The touch began: -1 none, 0 on the frame, 1 in the panel, 2 before the\n * menu came on (nobody's until it's let go: a finger still down from the\n * screen before isn't a press), 3 in the panel showing the map (the menu's:\n * letting go there is a press, NITRO_LOWERMENU_PANEL_PRESS). */\n```\n\nplus `4` = a tab and `5` = a panel button (lines 67–72). The routing is decided in `NitroPort_LowerMenuTouch` (line 2000) and `NitroPort_LowerMenuPanelAt` (line 1959):\n\n* A touch that **begins in the panel** (`NitroPort_LowerMenuPanelAt` returns 1) is the **game's**: `sTouchIn = 1` unless the panel is dark (`NitroPort_LowerMenuPanelFade() > 0` → 2), the map is shown (→ 3, the menu's press), or the app in the panel has its touch screen hidden (`sPanelTouch == 0` → 2, \"nobody's\").\n* A touch that begins **on a button** is the port's (`sTouchIn = 0`): the button shows pressed while the finger is on it; letting go on it makes a press (`sPress = button`), with `sPressDouble` set if it is the second press on that button within `NITRO_LOWERMENU_DOUBLE_FRAMES` (30).\n* The **panel's own buttons** (`panel_button_at()`, line 902) become `sTouchIn = 5` → press `NITRO_LOWERMENU_BUTTON_PRESS(k)`.\n* The **tabs** become `sTouchIn = 4` → press `NITRO_LOWERMENU_TAB_PRESS(k)`.\n* A touch in the panel showing the **map** is `sTouchIn = 3` → press `NITRO_LOWERMENU_PANEL_PRESS`.\n\nPress lifetime: `NitroPort_LowerMenuPressPending` (line 2117) drops a press older than `NITRO_LOWERMENU_PRESS_FRAMES` (30); `NitroPort_LowerMenuTakePress` (line 2130) consumes it.\n\n---\n\n## 4. The town map (`port_lowermap.c`)\n\n### 4.1 What it draws\n\nFrom the file header (`port_lowermap.c` lines 1–37):\n\n> \"The canvas is 256 x 247 DS pixels, made as the Town Map app makes its screens (the decompilation's `src/applications/town_map/`), from its own pictures in `graphic/tmap_gra.narc`:\n> - rows 0-191: its upper screen. BG3 the region's background (the sea and the blue bars, the name's bar), BG2 the land and the routes over it, blended (`G2_SetBlendAlpha(BG2, BG3, 28, 4)`: BG2 at 16/16, what's behind at 4/16); the hidden places shown copied into both as the Town Map does (`ShowHiddenLocation`), and the arrow of the Fly screen's bar taken out as it does for the Town Map item; the sprites (OBJ priority 2: in front of BG2 and BG3) as the game places them: the cursor (its two frames by turns), the player's head, one of the dots of the places been through before at a time, the towns' blocks; over everything, the name's window (BG1).\n> - rows 192-246: the guide page's rows 61-115 (the description's first lines): its zoomed-in map (BG3 its background, BG2 over it, 512 x 512, at the scroll the game gives) and the description's window over it.\n> Checked against the Town Map app's screens in the PC runner: the same pixels (2026-10-24).\"\n\n### 4.2 Where the data comes from\n\n* **The pictures**: `graphic/tmap_gra.narc`, read from the **data pack** (`load()`, line 278: `FS_OpenFile(&file, \"graphic/tmap_gra.narc\")`), parsed by `NitroPort_NarcMember` (line 122) and `NitroPort_NitroBlock` (line 161) — the port's own minimal NARC/RGCN reader. Member indices are hard-coded at lines 57–62 (`M_TOP_PAL`, `M_TOP_TILES`, `M_TOP_BG`, `M_HIDDEN_TOP`, `M_TOP_MAP`, `M_ZOOM_BG`, `M_ZOOM_MAP`, `M_HIDDEN_ZOOM`, …). The read happens **on the game's thread** (REMASTER 1787–1788: \"The Town Map's pictures are read on the game's thread (the data pack is its), once.\"), once: `NitroPort_LowerMapLoad()` → `load()`.\n* **The layout** (where the sprites are, which hidden places show, the zoomed-in map's scroll, the name and the description) comes from the **game**, through the plain calls `NitroPort_LowerMenuMapBegin/Sprite/Dot/Layout/Text/NoText/End` (patch 0033, revised in 0036). The game works the Town Map's own context out (`TownMapContext_Init`, `TOWN_MAP_MODE_ITEM`) and tells the port; the port does **not** read the game's map data itself.\n* The **texts** arrive as the game's window tiles (4 bits a pixel) plus a 16-colour palette; the port makes them pixels (`text_pixels()`, `port_lowermenu.c` line 1795; and in `port_lowermap.c` the name/description are copied into `sName`/`sDesc`).\n\n### 4.3 How it is updated\n\n* `NitroPort_LowerMapSet(map)` (line 852) compares the new map with the old and redraws **only what changed**: the whole canvas on the first map or when the hidden-places bitmask changes (`full`), the zoomed-in band (`band`) when the description or the zoom scroll changed, the dots' old and new rectangles, each sprite's old and new rectangle, and the name window's old and new rectangle. `NitroPort_LowerMapTakeDirty(&y0,&y1)` reports the panel rows redrawn.\n* Animations: the cursor has two frames (17 frames each, `CURSOR_FRAMES`), the dot shown changes every 26 frames (`DOT_FRAMES`): `NitroPort_LowerMapSetFrame(frame)` and `NitroPort_LowerMapFrameChanges(frame)` (line 960: `frame % 17 == 0 || frame % 26 == 0`).\n* The panel's picture is the canvas at 15/16 (240×232, each canvas pixel 2×2 texels, then bilinear) — `sPanel`, `NitroPort_LowerMapPanel()`.\n* The game only re-tells the map when the player's square or the place changes, or the field restarts: `StartMenu_PortShowPanel` (patch 0033/0036) compares `sPortMapStale`, the square `(x,z)` and the map header. REMASTER 1763–1773 quantifies the game's cost: \"On the PC runner a new square is about 0.03 ms of the game's time, a new place's texts about 0.06 and 0.1 ms on two frames (they were 1 ms in one, the drawing with them).\"\n\n---\n\n## 5. Input\n\n### 5.1 Touches\n\nThe platform calls the port **every frame** with the 3DS touch position:\n\n* 3DS (`main_3ds.c` lines 3127–3145):\n\n```\nif (sRemaster && (NitroPort_LowerMenuOn() || NitroPort_LowerMenuKeptShown()) && NitroPort_ComposeLowerMenuShown()) {\n    if (held & KEY_TOUCH) {\n        hidTouchRead(&touch);\n        if (NitroPort_LowerMenuTouch(1, touch.px, touch.py, &x, &y)) {\n            Platinum_SetTouch(1, x, y);\n        } else {\n            Platinum_SetTouch(0, 0, 0);\n        }\n    } else {\n        NitroPort_LowerMenuTouch(0, 0, 0, NULL, NULL);\n        Platinum_SetTouch(0, 0, 0);\n    }\n}\n```\n\n* PC runner (`main_pc.c` lines 1906–1921) — the same contract.\n\nSo the port is the **only** router: it decides whether the finger belongs to the lower panel or to the game, and it returns the **DS's lower-screen coordinates** (`*dsX`, `*dsY`, 0…255 / 0…191) when the game should have the touch.\n\nHow the decision is made:\n\n1. `NitroPort_LowerMenuPanelAt(x, y, &dsX, &dsY)` (line 1959) tests the panel rectangle (x 3…242, y 4…235) and converts the screen pixel to a **canvas** pixel: `cx = (2*(x-3)+1) * 256 / (2*240)`, `cy = (2*(y-4)+1) * 247 / (2*232)`; then to a DS row:\n   * with panel runs: `NitroPort_LowerMenuRunRow` gives the run; `FROM_LOWER` → the DS row is the run's source row; `FROM_UPPER` → the touch belongs to **nobody** (it keeps the last lower-screen position); no run → `cy -= NITRO_LOWERMENU_DS_ROW0` (27);\n   * tall mode: the canvas row *is* the DS row (the engine is 248 lines tall);\n   * finally clamped to 0…191.\n2. `NitroPort_LowerMenuTouch` then classifies the touch (see §3.6). A touch in the panel that the game should have returns **1** and the DS coordinates; a touch on a button returns **0** and the port keeps it (the game gets no touch at all).\n3. While the panel is dark (`NitroPort_LowerMenuPanelFade() > 0`) the panel's touches are nobody's (REMASTER 1699–1700: \"While the panel's dark its touches are nobody's.\").\n4. When an app whose touch screen is not shown is in the panel, the game says so with `NitroPort_LowerMenuSetPanelTouch(0)` (0035 for the bag, 0037 for the party/summary, 0039/0040 for the save/options pages) — the port then gives the game no touches at all in the panel.\n\n### 5.2 Button presses\n\nFace buttons and the D-pad are **not** routed by the port: they go to the game through the normal DS key path (`Platinum_SetButtons` at `main_3ds.c:3126`). The port-mode start menu reads them itself in `StartMenu_PortSelect` (patch 0032, lines 428–449 of the patch):\n\n```\n+    } else if (JOY_NEW(PAD_BUTTON_A) && sPortCursor >= 0) {\n+        Sound_PlayEffect(SE_CONFIRM_sseq_3);\n+        button = sPortCursor;\n+    } else if (JOY_NEW(PAD_BUTTON_B | PAD_BUTTON_X)) {\n+        Sound_PlayEffect(SE_CONFIRM_sseq_3);\n+        menu->state = START_MENU_STATE_END;\n+        return TRUE;\n+    } else {\n+        if (JOY_NEW(PAD_KEY_UP | PAD_KEY_DOWN) && sPortCursor >= 0) {\n```\n\n**X** opens the menu (patch 0032, `field_control.c: FieldInput_Update`: `if (pressedKeys & PAD_BUTTON_X) input->menu = TRUE;`), and a **tap** on a button opens it too (`StartMenu_PortTapOpens`).\n\n### 5.3 The press queue\n\nThe port records at most one pending press (`sPress`), with a 30-frame lifetime, and the game polls it:\n\n* `NitroPort_LowerMenuPressPending()` — read without consuming (used by the field to decide whether a tap opens the menu).\n* `NitroPort_LowerMenuTakePress()` — consume (used by the start menu's select).\n* `NitroPort_LowerMenuPressDouble()` — whether the last press was the second of two on the same button within 30 frames (the double tap that opens the Town Map app).\n\nPress codes: `0…7` the eight buttons, `8`/`9` the two squares (`NITRO_LOWERMENU_ITEM1/2`), `10` (`NITRO_LOWERMENU_PANEL_PRESS`) a tap on the map, `11 + tab` a tab, `11 + 4 + button` a panel button.\n\n---\n\n## 6. A minimal reimplementation plan for a GPU-native renderer\n\n### 6.1 What must be implemented (the port side)\n\nImplement the **same API** as `nitro_port_lowermenu.h` + `port_lowermap.h` with the same semantics, but backed by the GPU:\n\n1. **State** (mirroring `port_lowermenu.c` lines 30–137): available / on / keepShown / tall / panelShows / selected / held / enabled / female / items[2] / runs[12] / tabs[4] / panelButtons[32] / fade state machine (`fadeFrom`, `fadeTo`, `fadeStart`, `panelNext`, `dsWait`, `dsPop`) / the map hand-over chain. Keep the same locking discipline (spin-lock + `NitroPortPlatform_Sleep(50)` after 64 spins) if you keep a worker thread.\n2. **The menu picture** (320×240 RGBA8888). Two options:\n   * **(a) Keep the CPU raster** of `port_lowermenu.c` (`put`/`rect`/`box`/`text`/`paste`) and only change the *upload* path. Per-frame cost: **zero** when nothing changed (the picture is only redrawn on `redraw()`, i.e. on/off, cursor move, press, item change, tab change, enabled-mask change — see `NitroPort_LowerMenuSelect`, `SetEnabled`, `SetItem`, `SetFemale`, `Show`, `SetTabs`). Cost per redraw: ~76800 pixels × ~3 writes + a 307 KB memcpy ≈ 0.6–1.0 M pixel writes ≈ 0.5–1 ms on a Cortex-A9. Then a **307 KB texture upload** per redraw.\n   * **(b) GPU-native (recommended).** Bake the chrome into a 320×240 RGBA8 texture once and re-render only the changed part: the frame (2 quads + rounded corners), the 8 button cells (one quad each, with the selected/pressed variants), the 2 squares, the icons (8 icon quads), the names (a **glyph atlas**: 19 glyphs, 4×9, one texture; each label is 1–8 glyph quads ⇒ ≤ 40 quads), the tabs (≤ 4 quads + their labels). Per-frame steady-state cost: **one full-screen quad** (the menu texture) — nothing else. Per *change* cost: re-render + re-upload only the dirty region (a button cell is 67×22 px; a name is ~40×9 px). This is strictly cheaper than (a) and removes the 307 KB memcpy.\n3. **The panel's content**:\n   * the DS's lower screen: in `sinjoh` the DS screens are already rendered by the engine, so the panel is **one textured quad** (or three, for the top/bottom strip rows) sampling the lower screen's texture at 15/16 — no re-render, no CPU work;\n   * the map: reimplement `port_lowermap.c` as GPU work — the Town Map's BG2/BG3 are tilemaps over a tile texture (`tmap_gra.narc` NCGR + NCLR, already parsed by the port's NARC reader), so the upper screen is 2–4 textured quads (BG3 background, BG2 blended over it at 16/16 vs 4/16 ⇒ one quad with a 2-texture blend shader), the zoomed-in band is 2 more quads with a scroll, the sprites (cursor, head, blocks, dots) are ≤ 24+8 small quads, and the name/description windows are 2 quads of the game's 4bpp window tiles (uploaded as a tiny R4 texture, or converted to RGBA8 once). Steady-state per frame: **~10–40 quads**, no CPU raster.\n   * the runs-assembled canvas (trainer case): ≤ 12 quads, each sampling the lower or the upper screen's texture (plus the tab strip), so the canvas is never materialised.\n4. **Input**: the same `NitroPort_LowerMenuTouch` contract; the hit-testing arithmetic is trivial and can stay on the CPU.\n5. **The fade**: the same `PanelFade()` returning 0…16; the platform draws a black quad with that alpha over the panel — one quad, no texture.\n\n### 6.2 Per-frame cost, element by element\n\n| Element | Steady-state per frame | On change |\n|---|---|---|\n| Menu chrome (frame, 8 buttons, 2 squares, names, icons, tabs) | 1 quad (baked texture) — 0 if the menu is off | re-render of the changed cells + a partial texture upload (tens of KB) |\n| Panel showing the DS's lower screen | 3 quads sampling the lower screen's texture (top strip, 192 rows, bottom strip) | none |\n| Panel showing the map | ~10–40 quads (2 BG layers + band + sprites + 2 text windows) | the same, only when the map changes; animation frames only every 17/26 frames |\n| Panel assembled from runs (trainer case) | ≤ 12 quads | only when the runs change |\n| Fade | 1 alpha-blended black quad | — |\n| 3D inside the panel (the summary's Pokémon, the party's form change) | the engine's normal 3D pass, clipped to the panel | — |\n| Touch routing + press queue | O(1) CPU | — |\n| Map hand-over (`MapBegin…MapEnd`) | O(1) bookkeeping on the game's thread | the drawer thread does the drawing |\n\n### 6.3 What can be reused unchanged\n\n* **The whole patch series 0031–0041** — the game-side code is engine-agnostic; it only calls the `NitroPort_LowerMenu*` API and the game's own functions. If `sinjoh` exports the same symbols with the same semantics, the patches apply verbatim.\n* The **game's own rendering** of the bag/party/summary/save/options/trainer-case into the DS's lower screen (and the tall layout) — in `sinjoh` the DS 2D engine is native, so `NitroPort_LowerMenuSetTall` must be honoured by the engine's split (`NitroRender2DSplit.height = 248`), the same way `port_render2d.c` does it.\n* The **NARC/RGCN reader** (`NitroPort_NarcMember`, `NitroPort_NitroBlock`) — small, self-contained, and exactly what the map and the icons need.\n* The **layout constants** (panel rectangle, canvas size, button column geometry, `NITRO_LOWERMENU_DS_ROW0`, `NITRO_LOWERMENU_TALL_LINES`) and the **hit-testing arithmetic** (`canvas_row`, `panel_button_at`, `tab_at`).\n\n### 6.4 What must be re-specified (contract details that are easy to get wrong)\n\n* `NitroPort_LowerMenuShow` must reset `sTall`, `sPanelTouch`, the tabs and the panel runs/buttons on turning off.\n* The press lifetime (30 frames), the double-tap window (30 frames), the press codes (buttons 0–7, squares 8–9, panel 10, tabs 11+, panel buttons 15+).\n* The fade semantics: 8 frames per whole fade (`NITRO_LOWERMENU_FADE_FRAMES`), 16 levels, `CLEAR_NOW` = −1, the 4-frame hold for the DS's lower screen (`FADE_DS_HOLD`), the 30-frame wait for the map (`FADE_WAIT_MAX`).\n* `NitroPort_LowerMenuPanelFade()` must be callable **every frame** by the display thread and must complete a pending `FadeToPanel` change exactly once, when the panel is black.\n* `NitroPort_LowerMenuMapText`'s 0036 signature (`tiles`, `palette`, `key`) and `NitroPort_LowerMenuMapTextKept`'s LRU-of-8 behaviour (the game prints the texts only once per key; the port keeps the last 8 of each).\n\n---\n\n## 7. Open questions and risks\n\n### 7.1 Things that cannot be copied directly\n\n1. **The menu's own rasterizer.** `port_lowermenu.c`'s `put`/`rect`/`box`/`text`/`text_outlined`/`paste`/`shrink` is a hand-written **CPU** rasterizer writing into `sDraw[320*240]` (307 KB). It is *not* p3ds's software 2D renderer (`port_render2d.c`), but it is CPU rasterization and must be replaced by GPU work (or kept and paid for only on change).\n2. **The Town Map's rasterizer.** `port_lowermap.c` rasterises a 256×247 canvas on the CPU (`bg_row`, `draw_back_top`, `draw_back_band`, `draw_sprite`, `scale_rect`) and then scales it to 240×232 (`widened_row`, `mix`, `widen`). It is only redrawn when something changes, but it is a CPU rasterizer and it is the biggest CPU cost in the feature.\n3. **The DS's lower screen inside the panel** depends on p3ds's **software** 2D renderer: `3ds_port/nitro/README.md` line 40 says \"**2D graphics | both engines drawn in software: text, affine and extended BGs … `NitroPort_RenderScreens` gives the two screens as 15-bit pixels | `src/port_render2d.c` |**\". In `sinjoh` the DS screens are native, so the panel is a texture blit — but then the *panel's* content is no longer the DS's pixels but the engine's, and the layout constants (`DS_ROW0 27`, 15/16 scale) must be reproduced.\n4. **The compositor's panel drawing** (`port_compose_pica.c`: the menu texture, the map texture, the panel pieces, the fade quad, the \"upper screen kept\" logic) is p3ds-specific; `sinjoh` needs its own compositor path for the lower screen, including the \"upper screen kept as it is\" behaviour (`NitroPort_LowerMenuHoldUpper`) and the 3D-in-the-panel clipping.\n\n### 7.2 New-3DS-specific hardware dependencies\n\n* **The map drawer thread**: on a New 3DS it runs on the second core at the lowest priority (`main_3ds.c` lines 2270–2315, `NitroPort_LowerMenuSetMapWorker(MapWake)`); on an Old 3DS it is core 0 (REMASTER 1776–1780: \"on the 3DS a thread at the lowest priority on a New 3DS's second core (core 0 on an Old 3DS)\"). REMASTER also records the reason: \"walking with the map out costs the game's thread next to nothing … still a hitch on the 3DS, its core 0 nearly full\". A GPU-native engine may not need a worker at all (the map could be a texture updated on the GPU), but the API contract (`MapWork` returning \"1 if it drew something\", the serial numbers) must still be honoured if the patches are reused.\n* The **3DS texture memory**: the menu's picture (320×240 RGBA8 = 307 KB) and the map's (240×232 RGBA8 = 223 KB) live in the PICA's VRAM, double-buffered (\"two taken by turns\", REMASTER 1721–1724). `sinjoh` has its own texture budget.\n* The **PICA's blitting** of the DS's picture into the panel: \"the compositor puts it in a texture (RGB565, a texel a pixel, two taken by turns, each brought up to date with only the rows it's behind on)\" — the RGB565 conversion and the 8-row tile alignment (`y0 & ~7`) are p3ds-specific details of `port_compose_pica.c`'s `menu_texture()`.\n\n### 7.3 Genuine inconsistencies found in the sources\n\n* **`NitroPort_LowerMenuHoldLower` exists only in patches 0035 and 0036.** It is declared and used in 0035 (`bag/main.c`, `start_menu.c`) and **removed** by 0036, which deletes every use (`-extern void NitroPort_LowerMenuHoldLower(int hold);` and the calls). The current `include/nitro_port_lowermenu.h` has **no** `HoldLower`, and `port_lowermenu.c` implements none — consistent, because the patches are applied in order and 0036 removes the dependency. But a new engine that applies only 0035 must provide a `HoldLower` stub; a new engine that applies the whole series does not need it at all.\n* **`NitroPort_LowerMenuMapText` changes signature between 0033 and 0036** (from returning a `u16*` buffer to taking the tiles + palette + key). The final contract is the 0036 one; the 0033 form must not be implemented.\n* **`NitroPort_LowerMenuKeptShown`** is introduced by 0037, not 0036, although 0036's text refers to keeping the menu on.\n* `NitroPort_LowerMenuSetPanelRuns` in patch 0038 is declared with the *game's* types (`TrainerCasePortRun`, `TrainerCasePortTabStyle`) — the port's own types are `NitroLowerPanelRun` / `NitroLowerTabStyle` in `nitro_port_lowermenu.h`; the patch's local structs must be layout-compatible. This is a porting trap worth checking.\n* The **panel's tabs** in the trainer case are drawn by the **port** (`draw_tabs()`, `port_lowermenu.c` line 979) using the port's own font, bold, with a small Poké Ball — but the tab *rows* are part of the runs (`NITRO_LOWERMENU_FROM_TABS`), so the canvas has a hole where the tabs go that the port fills from its own picture.\n\n### 7.4 Not answered by the sources\n\n* The **exact pixel layout of the panel's frame** (the mock-up of 2026-10-23) is only described in prose in `port_lowermenu.c` (`draw()`, lines 745–843) and in REMASTER; there is no separate layout document in this repository, so a faithful re-implementation must copy `draw()`'s geometry and colours verbatim (or diff against the PC runner's `mshot` output).\n* **Why the menu is 15/16** and the exact bilinear filter used by the compositor are p3ds compositor details (`port_compose_pica.c`), not part of the port API; `sinjoh` will have to choose its own sampling.\n* The **cost of the whole feature on the 3DS** is not measured in the sources; the only numbers are the game's side of the map (\"about 0.03 ms … 0.06 and 0.1 ms\", REMASTER 1771–1773) and the observation that the 3DS \"core 0 nearly full\" while the map is out (REMASTER 1762).\n\n---\n\n### One-paragraph summary\n\nThe feature is: in the field, the 3DS's lower screen becomes the port's own menu picture — a 320×240 frame with a 240×232 panel on the left (showing the game's own DS lower screen, or the Town Map, or a bag/party/summary/trainer-case/save/options app drawn tall) and a column of eight buttons plus two item squares on the right. The game side is eleven patches (0031–0041) that call a **single, well-documented C API** (`NitroPort_LowerMenu*` in `include/nitro_port_lowermenu.h`, `NitroPort_LowerMap*` in `src/port_lowermap.h`); the port side is one CPU-rasterized picture (`port_lowermenu.c`), one CPU-rasterized Town Map (`port_lowermap.c`), a fade state machine, a touch router with a one-deep press queue, and a hand-over chain that moves the map drawing off the game's thread. A GPU-native engine can keep the whole patch series and the whole API unchanged; what it must replace is the picture rasterization (bake the chrome into a texture, re-render only changed cells), the Town Map rasterization (tilemap + sprite quads from `tmap_gra.narc`), and the compositor's panel composition (quads instead of CPU row copies) — while preserving the exact semantics of the fade, the press queue, the touch routing, and the dirty-row/serial protocol.\n</subagent>",

NitroPort_HBlankLinesOnce(void)\\r\\n{\\r\\n    /* The game arms its \r\nH-blank DMAs again only in its V-blank interrupt:\\r\\n     * a second time, they'd carry on past their tables (and the \r\nhandlers\\r\\n     * run twice as often). */\\r\\n    if (sLinesVBlank == sVBlanks) {\\r\\n        return FALSE;\\r\\n    \r\n}\\r\\n    sLinesVBlank = sVBlanks;\\r\\n    NitroPort_HBlankLines();\\r\\n    return \r\nTRUE;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n__attribute__((weak)) void NitroPort_OnFrame(void)\\r\\n{\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n__attribute__((weak)) void \r\nNitroPort_VBlankWorkDone(void)\\r\\n{\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n/* V-blank starts: its interrupt is requested and V-blank DMAs run \r\n(masked\\r\\n * meanwhile, so the interrupts are then taken lowest first). */\\r\\nstatic void StartVBlank(void)\\r\\n{\\r\\n  \r\n  u32 saved = OSi_PortCpsr;\\r\\n\\r\\n    OSi_PortCpsr |= HW_PSR_IRQ_DISABLE;\\r\\n    sVBlanks++;\\r\\n    \r\nNitroPort_VBlankStarts();\\r\\n    NitroPort_GxRefresh();\\r\\n    reg_OS_IF |= OS_IE_V_BLANK;\\r\\n    \r\nNitroPort_DmaVBlank();\\r\\n    OSi_PortCpsr = saved;\\r\\n    NitroPort_RaiseIrq(0);\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n/* DS time spent this \r\nframe on work the port does instantly (game card\\r\\n * reads); see NitroPort_SpendDsTime. */\\r\\nstatic u64 \r\nsWorkCycles;\\r\\n\\r\\n/* NitroSystem's \u001b[7mVRAM\u001b[0m transfer manager, when the program has it\\r\\n * (patches/NitroSystem/0004): \r\nthe 3D transfers queued for the V-blank. */\\r\\nextern void NNSi_GfdDoVramTransfer3D(void) \r\n__attribute__((weak));\\r\\n\\r\\n__attribute__((weak)) void NitroPort_Halt(void)\\r\\n{\\r\\n    /* The DS sleeps until an \r\ninterrupt arrives. In a game the next one is\\r\\n     * (almost always) V-blank, so: finish this frame, then raise it. \r\nIf the\\r\\n     * CPU has interrupts masked (OS_WaitInterrupt, OS_Terminate), it wakes\\r\\n     * up but doesn't take \r\nthem: they stay pending until it unmasks them. */\\r\\n\\r\\n    /* The DS draws the 3D scene the game has just ended \r\nafter the V-blank\\r\\n     * work, which does the texture transfers the game queued for it; the\\r\\n     * port draws it \r\nnow. So those are done now. Unless the 3D drawing is\\r\\n     * behind and a scene from before may still be drawn: that \r\none would\\r\\n     * get them too, so the V-blank work does them then, as on the DS. */\\r\\n    if \r\n(NNSi_GfdDoVramTransfer3D != NULL && !NitroPort_Gx3dEarlierSceneUnread()) {\\r\\n        NNSi_GfdDoVramTransfer3D();\\r\\n \r\n   }\\r\\n    NitroPort_OnFrame();\\r\\n    sWorkCycles = 0;\\r\\n    StartVBlank();\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nvoid \r\nNitroPort_SpendDsTime(u64 cycles)\\r\\n{\\r\\n    /* A long load takes the DS several frames, and V-blank interrupts \r\nkeep\\r\\n     * coming meanwhile: the game relies on them, e.g. its V-blank task\\r\\n     * list (32 entries) is emptied \r\nby the V-blank handler while a field\\r\\n=== platform 3ds ===\\r\\n6: * others wait on their signal; see \r\nsrc/port_thread.c), so the 3DS\\r\\n34: void NitroPortPlatform_Wait(NitroPortSignal *signal)\\r\\n95: uint64_t \r\nNitroPortPlatform_Nanoseconds(void)\\r\\n104: void NitroPortPlatform_Sleep(uint32_t microseconds)\\r\\n106: /* \r\n(svcSleepThread(0) would only let threads of the same priority run) */\\r\\n107: svcSleepThread((s64)(microseconds ? \r\nmicroseconds : 1) * 1000);\\r\\n\"\r\ndocs\\chatlog00.md:18486:                \"text\": \"/*\\r\\n * kj_frame.c: the scheduling bridge between the game's DS \r\nframe and the\\r\\n * 3DS presentation (DS side).\\r\\n *\\r\\n * One emulated DS V-blank is one physical 3DS V-blank: the \r\ngame's OS_Halt\\r\\n * (NitroPort_Halt -> NitroPort_OnFrame) waits for the 3DS display. HGSS's\\r\\n * main loop waits \r\ntwice per game frame, so the game naturally runs at\\r\\n * ~29.9 game frames a second and nothing here doubles or \r\nhalves it.\\r\\n *\\r\\n * The frame is published once per game frame, at the point patch 2001\\r\\n * marks in NitroMain \r\n(after the V-blank callback, the sound update and the\\r\\n * vwait task queue): the game is stopped at its frame \r\nboundary, so the\\r\\n * renderer reads one coherent version of registers, palettes, OAM and \u001b[7mVRAM\u001b[0m\\r\\n * on this thread, \r\nand nothing races it. Loops that wait for V-blank without\\r\\n * reaching that point (soft-reset and error screens, the \r\nfew boot frames)\\r\\n * are published from the V-blank itself after a short grace period.\\r\\n */\\r\\n\\r\\n#include \r\n\\\"kj_bridge.h\\\"\\r\\n#include \\\"kj_g3.h\\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n#include <nitro.h>\\r\\n#include <nitro_port.h>\\r\\n#include \r\n<string.h>\\r\\n\\r\\nextern unsigned char NitroPort_IoReg[];\\r\\nextern unsigned char NitroPort_Pltt[];\\r\\nextern unsigned \r\nchar NitroPort_Oam[];\\r\\nextern unsigned char NitroPort_BgVram[];\\r\\nextern unsigned char \r\nNitroPort_DbBgVram[];\\r\\nextern unsigned char NitroPort_ObjVram[];\\r\\nextern unsigned char \r\nNitroPort_DbObjVram[];\\r\\nextern unsigned char NitroPort_LcdcVram[];\\r\\n\\r\\nvoid \r\nNitroPort_SoundPumpReplies(void);\\r\\nextern u64 svcGetSystemTick(void);\\r\\n\\r\\nstatic u64 s_pump_ticks, \r\ns_hblank_ticks;\\r\\nstatic u32 s_pump_calls, s_hblank_walks;\\r\\nstatic u64 s_sync_calls_base, \r\ns_sync_ticks_base;\\r\\n\\r\\n/* V-blanks without a publish after which the V-blank publishes itself. Two\\r\\n * is the \r\nmain loop's normal cadence; four leaves room for a frame that\\r\\n * overran once. */\\r\\n#define PUBLISH_GRACE_VBLANKS \r\n4u\\r\\n\\r\\nstatic kj_ds_memory s_memory;\\r\\nstatic u32 s_vblanks;\\r\\nstatic u32 s_publishes;\\r\\nstatic u32 \r\ns_last_publish_vblank;\\r\\n\\r\\nstatic const u32 BANK_LCDC_OFFSET[9] = {\\r\\n    0x00000, 0x20000, 0x40000, 0x60000, \r\n0x80000, 0x90000, 0x94000, 0x98000, 0xA0000,\\r\\n};\\r\\nstatic const u32 BANK_SIZE[9] = {\\r\\n    0x20000, 0x20000, \r\n0x20000, 0x20000, 0x10000, 0x4000, 0x4000, 0x8000, 0x4000,\\r\\n};\\r\\n/* VRAMCNT_A..G are 0x240..0x246, H and I \r\n0x248/0x249 (0x247 is WRAMCNT). */\\r\\nstatic const u16 BANK_REG[9] = {\\r\\n    0x240, 0x241, 0x242, 0x243, 0x244, \r\n0x245, 0x246, 0x248, 0x249,\\r\\n};\\r\\n\\r\\nconst kj_ds_memory *kj_ds_get_memory(void)\\r\\n{\\r\\n    if (s_memory.io == \r\nNULL) {\\r\\n        s_memory.io = NitroPort_IoReg;\\r\\n        s_memory.io_size = HW_IOREG_SIZE;\\r\\n        \r\ns_memory.pltt = NitroPort_Pltt;\\r\\n        s_memory.oam = NitroPort_Oam;\\r\\n        s_memory.bg_vram_a = \r\nNitroPort_BgVram;\\r\\n        s_memory.bg_vram_b = NitroPort_DbBgVram;\\r\\n        s_memory.obj_vram_a = \r\nNitroPort_ObjVram;\\r\\n        s_memory.obj_vram_b = NitroPort_DbObjVram;\\r\\n        s_memory.lcdc_vram = \r\nNitroPort_LcdcVram;\\r\\n    }\\r\\n    return &s_memory;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nstatic void decode_banks(kj_vram_bank \r\nbanks[9])\\r\\n{\\r\\n    for (int i = 0; i < 9; ++i) {\\r\\n        const u8 cnt = NitroPort_IoReg[BANK_REG[i]];\\r\\n\\r\\n    \r\n    banks[i].lcdc_offset = BANK_LCDC_OFFSET[i];\\r\\n        banks[i].size = BANK_SIZE[i];\\r\\n        banks[i].enabled = \r\n(cnt & 0x80) != 0;\\r\\n        banks[i].mst = cnt & 0x07;\\r\\n        banks[i].ofs = (cnt >> 3) & 0x03;\\r\\n    \r\n}\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nstatic void publish(void)\\r\\n{\\r\\n    kj_frame_input in;\\r\\n\\r\\n    /* The per-line registers of this \r\nframe: H-blank handlers and DMAs run\\r\\n     * once per V-blank, after the game's V-blank work armed them. */\\r\\n    \r\n{\\r\\n#ifndef HGSS_PROFILE_OFF\\r\\n        const u64 t0 = svcGetSystemTick();\\r\\n#endif\\r\\n        if \r\n(NitroPort_HBlankLinesOnce()) {\\r\\n#ifndef HGSS_PROFILE_OFF\\r\\n            ++s_hblank_walks;\\r\\n#endif\\r\\n        \r\n}\\r\\n#ifndef HGSS_PROFILE_OFF\\r\\n        s_hblank_ticks += svcGetSystemTick() - t0;\\r\\n#endif\\r\\n    }\\r\\n\\r\\n    \r\nmemset(&in, 0, sizeof(in));\\r\\n    in.mem = kj_ds_get_memory();\\r\\n    decode_banks(in.banks);\\r\\n    in.lines.active \r\n= NitroPort_LineRegs.active != 0;\\r\\n    in.lines.regs = in.lines.active\\r\\n                        ? (const uint8_t \r\n(*)[192][KJ_LINE_REG_BYTES])NitroPort_LineRegs.regs\\r\\n                        : NULL;\\r\\n    in.g3 = \r\nkj_g3_take_frame();\\r\\n    in.vblank_count = s_vblanks;\\r\\n    in.game_frame = ++s_publishes;\\r\\n    \r\nin.engine_a_on_top = NitroPort_EngineAOnTop() != FALSE;\\r\\n    s_last_publish_vblank = s_vblanks;\\r\\n    \r\nkj_ctr_publish_frame(&in);\\r\\n    kj_g3_set_capture(kj_ctr_capture_next_frame());\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nvoid \r\nNitroPort_VBlankWorkDone(void)\\r\\n{\\r\\n    publish();\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nvoid NitroPort_OnFrame(void)\\r\\n{\\r\\n    const \r\nkj_input *input;\\r\\n\\r\\n    ++s_vblanks;\\r\\n    {\\r\\n#ifndef HGSS_PROFILE_OFF\\r\\n        const u64 t0 = \r\nsvcGetSystemTick();\\r\\n#endif\\r\\n        NitroPort_SoundPumpReplies();\\r\\n#ifndef HGSS_PROFILE_OFF\\r\\n        \r\ns_pump_ticks += svcGetSystemTick() - t0;\\r\\n        ++s_pump_calls;\\r\\n#endif\\r\\n    }\\r\\n\\r\\n    if \r\n(!kj_ctr_vblank()) {\\r\\n        NitroPort_Log(\\\"[kj] close requested at V-blank %lu\\\", (unsigned long)s_vblanks);\\r\\n  \r\n      NitroPort_CardFlush();\\r\\n        kj_ctr_terminate();\\r\\n    }\\r\\n\\r\\n    input = kj_ctr_input();\\r\\n    \r\nNitroPort_SetButtons(input->keys, FALSE);\\r\\n    NitroPort_SetTouch(input->touch ? TRUE : FALSE, input->touch_x, \r\ninput->touch_y);\\r\\n\\r\\n    if (s_vblanks - s_last_publish_vblank > PUBLISH_GRACE_VBLANKS) {\\r\\n        publish();\\r\\n \r\n   }\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n/* POWCNT1 (0x04000304) bit 15: engine A drives the upper screen. */\\r\\nBOOL \r\nNitroPort_EngineAOnTop(void)\\r\\n{\\r\\n    return (NitroPort_IoReg[0x305] & 0x80) ? TRUE : FALSE;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nvoid \r\nNitroPort_Terminate(void)\\r\\n{\\r\\n    NitroPort_Log(\\\"[kj] the game terminated itself (OS_Terminate)\\\");\\r\\n    \r\nNitroPort_CardFlush();\\r\\n    kj_ctr_terminate();\\r\\n}\\r\\n\"\r\ndocs\\chatlog00.md:18825:          \"text\": \"The coffeepot performance page confirms measurement approach. Once the \r\nbuild finishes, run again and check [gpu]/[pace] counters.\\n\\nI could add a 30Hz present cadence now: only call \r\npublish every other game frame. But careful: kohjoh's renderer scrapes state at publish; if we skip a publish, the \r\nnext publish captures the state of that frame, which is fine for presentation, but 3D scene capture must not be \r\nskipped for frames the game discards? For field/title producers, kj_ctr_capture_next_frame is set at end of publish; \r\nskipping publish means capture stays as set... The G3 interpreter capture logic may need per-frame. Safer to publish \r\nevery frame but skip GPU presentation every other. But that doubles CPU capture work.\\n\\nActually kohjoh's design: \r\npublish every game frame; renderer draws; if behind �2 skip one. For 30fps O3DS we want to draw every 2nd frame but \r\nstill capture? The capture is the expensive CPU part (G3 decode). If we skip drawing, we can also skip capture via \r\nkj_ctr_capture_next_frame() returning false. But the game keeps producing scenes; if we don't capture, the next \r\ncaptured frame is fresh (game state at that point), which is fine.\\n\\nHowever, the 2D atlas requires reading \u001b[7mVRAM\u001b[0m at \r\npublish. Skipping a publish means the state at the next publish reflects the newer frame - fine.\\n\\nSo implement 30Hz: \r\nin publish(), if `(s_vblanks & 1)` skip? But that must not break animation/input timing. Presentation at 30Hz while \r\ngame ticks 60Hz is intended.\\n\\nWait: the user's baseline is \\\"stable 30 Hz presentation\\\". The renderer in kohjoh \r\nmight already present every frame at 60. On O3DS, if we draw 60 frames/s, GPU load doubles. So an explicit O3DS \r\ncadence is needed. Add a compile-time/default runtime setting: present every 2nd publish. But then the game's V-blank \r\ntiming unaffected.\\n\\nImplementation detail: `publish()` does capture (H-blank lines, G3 take frame, decode banks) \r\nthen calls renderer. To skip draw, we can still capture but pass to renderer which skips? Better: if skipping, don't \r\ncall publish at all; but we must keep s_last_publish_vblank updated so grace path doesn't fire. Set \r\ns_last_publish_vblank = s_vblanks on skip.\\n\\nBut there's a catch: `kj_g3_set_capture(kj_ctr_capture_next_frame())` \r\ncontrols whether the DS-side G3 interpreter records the next scene. If we never publish on a skipped frame, capture \r\nstays enabled from last publish \u001a records scenes we won't draw, wasting CPU. Set capture false on skipped frames, then \r\ntrue before a drawn frame. But the game may have already produced the scene before we know. The G3 interpreter keeps \r\nthe \\\"last swapped\\\" scene; if skipping a frame, capture remains on. Complex. kohjoh's existing policy already skips \r\nonly when behind.       "text": "Instructions from: C:\\Users\\terezi\\workdir\\coffeepot\\AGENTS.md\n# AGENTS.md — coffeepot\n\nCoffeepot is a wiki for research on Nintendo consoles: their hardware, their software, and homebrew development.\n\nIt serves two readers: a curious human, and a future coding agent doing hardware/software work on these consoles. Every page must work for both.\n\n## Repository layout\n\n```text\nAGENTS.md\nzensical.toml               # site config: navigation, theme, and what is excluded\nglossary.md                  # global jargon glossary\nREADME.md                    # human landing page (what this wiki covers)\n<console>/                   # one directory per console platform (e.g. ctr/, nx/)\n  index.md                   # console overview + hub\n  glossary.md                # per-device jargon glossary\n  hardware/<topic>.md        # one page per hardware component/system\n  software/<topic>.md        # one page per system software / format / service\n  homebrew/<topic>.md        # one page per exploit / tool / library / workflow\n  engineering/<topic>.md     # one page per practical problem (debugging, performance, porting...)\n  benchmarks/<name>/         # buildable benchmark programs + README.md with method and results\ntools/\n  check_docs.py              # link, anchor and Sources-section checker\n  build_benchmarks.sh        # builds every benchmark, fails on warnings\nsite/                        # generated site output (not committed)\n```\n\nCurrent scope is three platforms: `ctr/` (Nintendo 3DS family), `nx/` (Nintendo Switch family) and `oz/` (Nintendo Switch 2 family). Add a new top-level platform directory only for a distinct hardware platform, using its established codename or short kebab-case name (e.g. `ctr`, `nx`, `oz`).\n\nFile names are kebab-case: `arm9-cpu.md`, `nand-filesystem.md`, `boot9strap.md`. One topic per file.\n\n## Core principles\n\n1. **Don't repeat yourself. Link instead.** If something is already explained on another page, summarize it in at most 1–2 sentences and link to the canonical page. Never copy a full explanation into two places.\n2. **Write like a human.** Natural, plain language first. Short paragraphs. Active voice. A motivated non-expert should be able to follow the Overview of any page.\n3. **Minimal jargon, full technical detail.** Avoid jargon unless it names something precisely. When jargon is necessary, define it once, link it to a glossary, then use it freely. Never simplify away technical facts (registers, addresses, versions, file offsets, behaviors) to sound readable — push them into a `Technical details` section instead of dropping them.\n4. **Progressive disclosure.** Plain-language summary up top, exhaustive detail below. Human reads the top; agent reads the whole page.\n\n## Jargon and glossaries\n\nJargon means any term a non-expert would stumble on: acronyms (`SoC`, `IPC`), Nintendo-specific codenames (`CTR`, `Horizon`), homebrew terms (`CFW`, `ROP`), and hardware terms used in a precise sense (`physical address`, `kernel privilege`).\n\nRules:\n\n- On first use in a page, give the plain meaning, then the term in bold with a glossary link. Example: `the main chip that combines CPU and GPU (a **system-on-a-chip**, or **[SoC](../../glossary.md#soc)**)`. After that, just use `SoC`.\n- Every jargon term used on a page must resolve to exactly one glossary entry: either the global glossary or that console's glossary.\n- **Global `glossary.md`**: terms with the same meaning across two or more consoles, or general computing terms (`CPU`, `GPU`, `kernel`, `firmware`, `NAND`, `ARM`). Define once here.\n- **Per-device `<console>/glossary.md`**: terms specific to one console (`boot9strap`, `Horizon`, `PICA200`). Define here.\n- If a per-device term starts being used by pages for a second console with the same meaning, promote it to the global glossary and leave a pointer link behind in the per-device glossary.\n- Glossary entries are short: 1–4 sentences of plain meaning, plus the precise technical sense in one more sentence if needed, plus a link to the canonical wiki page for the full story. Never put the full explanation in the glossary; the glossary points at pages, pages point back at the glossary.\n\nGlossary entry format:\n\n```markdown\n<a name=\"anchor-slug\"></a>\n\n### Term name\n\nOne to four sentences: what it is in plain language, then the precise sense. Ends with a link to the canonical page.\n\nExample: <a name=\"soc\"></a>\n\n### System-on-a-chip (SoC)\n```\n\n## Page types\n\nPick exactly one type per page. If a topic spans types (e.g. a chip and its SDK driver), split into linked pages rather than one blended page.\n\n- `<console>/index.md` — console overview and hub. What the console is, when it was sold, what makes it distinctive, spec summary (as a table of links, not raw numbers repeated from subpages), software landscape, homebrew state. Links to every major subpage.\n- `hardware/<topic>.md` — one hardware component or subsystem (CPU, GPU, memory map, display, input, cartridge, wireless). What it does, where it sits in the system, its observable behavior, then full specs.\n- `software/<topic>.md` — one software thing (OS/kernel, system menu, applet, file format, filesystem, system service, update mechanism). What the user sees, what a developer needs to know, formats and behaviors.\n- `homebrew/<topic>.md` — one exploit, custom firmware, tool, library, or workflow. What it achieves, who it is for, how it works, how to use it, limits and risks.\n- `engineering/<topic>.md` — one practical problem a developer faces when writing software for the console (debugging, profiling, performance, memory management, rendering, asset conversion, hardware testing). Reference pages say what the hardware and libraries *are*; engineering pages say how to *use* them in working software and how to check the result. They link to the reference pages for facts rather than restating them.\n\n## Templates\n\nCopy the matching template. Delete sections that genuinely don't apply, but never delete `Technical details` or `Sources` — if detail is unknown, say what is unknown.\n\n### Console index\n\n```markdown\n# <Console common name>\n\nPlain-language overview: what this console is, when it was sold, what makes it notable. 3–6 sentences.\n\n## At a glance\n\n| Area | Summary |\n| ---- | ------- |\n| CPU | [One-line plain summary](hardware/<page>.md) |\n| GPU / video | [One-line plain summary](hardware/<page>.md) |\n| Memory | [One-line plain summary](hardware/<page>.md) |\n| Storage / media | [One-line plain summary](hardware/<page>.md) |\n| Operating software | [One-line plain summary](software/<page>.md) |\n| Homebrew status | 1–2 sentences + link to key [homebrew page](homebrew/<page>.md) |\n\nKeep numbers out of this table unless they fit in one line. Full specs live on subpages.\n\n## Hardware\n\nBulleted list of subpages with one plain sentence each: [Page](hardware/<page>.md) — what it covers.\n\n## Software\n\nSame: [Page](software/<page>.md) — what it covers.\n\n## Homebrew\n\nSame: [Page](homebrew/<page>.md) — what it achieves and who it is for.\n\n## Notes and open questions\n\nAnything uncertain, disputed, or TODO. Be explicit: what is unknown, what would answer it.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [Title](URL) — what this source covers\n```\n\n### Hardware page\n\n```markdown\n# <Component name>\n\nPlain-language overview: what this part does and why it matters. 3–6 sentences. No unexplained acronyms here.\n\n## Where it fits\n\nHow this component connects to the rest of the system (1 short paragraph + links to neighboring pages). Use tables for registers/specs. Do not simplify here. If a value differs by model or firmware, give the table, not a single number.\n\n## Homebrew notes\n\nWhat a homebrew developer needs: how to access this hardware, what libraries/registers/services expose it, common pitfalls. 1–2 sentences + links if the full workflow lives on a [homebrew page](../homebrew/<page>.md).\n\n## Sources\n\n- [Title](URL) — what this source covers\n```\n\n### Software page\n\n```markdown\n# <Software / format / service name>\n\nPlain-language overview: what the user sees, what it is for. 3–6 sentences.\n\n## Behavior\n\nWhat it does, when it runs, how it interacts with other software/hardware. Plain language, linked jargon.\n\n## Technical details\n\nFull detail: versions, file layouts, offsets, headers, cryptographic checks, IPC interfaces, error behavior, version differences. Tables over prose for formats.\n\n## Homebrew notes\n\nHow homebrew interacts with this: patched, replaced, abused, or avoided — and links to the relevant [homebrew pages](../homebrew/<page>.md).\n\n## Sources\n\n- [Title](URL) — what this source covers\n```\n\n### Homebrew page\n\n```markdown\n# <Exploit / tool / library name>\n\nPlain-language overview: what this achieves and who it is for (player, developer). 2–4 sentences. State the required console, firmware range, and outcome in the first paragraph.\n\n## What you need\n\nConsole model(s), firmware version range, files, prior setup. Be exact; version ranges are technical facts, not trivia.\n\n## How it works\n\nHigh-level mechanism first (plain language, 1 paragraph), then the precise chain: entry point, escalation, persistence. Link each stage to the relevant hardware/software pages instead of re-explaining them.\n\n## Technical details\n\nFull detail: offsets, payloads, addresses, file hashes if relevant, failure modes, version-specific differences.\n\n## Limits and risks\n\nWhat it cannot do, what can brick or ban, what undoes it (updates, resets). Be blunt.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [Title](URL) — what this source covers (upstream repo, write-up, release notes)\n```\n\n### Engineering page\n\n```markdown\n# <Problem-oriented title, e.g. \"Debugging homebrew\">\n\nPlain-language overview: which problem this page solves, who hits it, and the short answer. 2–4 sentences.\n\n## Before you start\n\nToolchain and library versions the page was checked against, console models it applies to, prior setup.\n\n## <Task sections>\n\nOne section per task or decision, in the order a developer meets them. Each gives: what to do, a minimal code or command example, what result to expect, and how it fails. Link to the reference pages for hardware facts.\n\n## Technical details\n\nExact API behaviour (with the source file it was read from), constants, edge cases, model differences.\n\n## Pitfalls\n\nMistakes that cost people time, each with its symptom and fix.\n\n## Open questions\n\nWhat has not been measured or verified, and what experiment would settle it.\n\n## Sources\n\n- [Title](URL) — what this source covers\n```\n\n## Console setup and development scope\n\nFor 3DS custom-firmware installation, updates, recovery and backup procedures, direct readers to the [3DS Hacks Guide](https://3ds.hacks.guide/); do not maintain parallel installation instructions here. Keep historical and technical explanations of exploits, bootloaders and firmware. Coffeepot covers the development toolchain and writing, running, debugging and testing homebrew once the console is ready; emulator-based development can begin without a modified console.\n\n## Console models: Old 3DS is the default\n\nFor `ctr/`, every statement, number, example and recommendation describes the **Old 3DS** unless it says otherwise. Never assume a New 3DS. Anything that applies only to the New 3DS, or that differs on it, goes in an explicit **New 3DS** disclaimer after the Old 3DS statement.\n\n- **Terminology.** Use exactly \"Old 3DS\" and \"New 3DS\" (capitalised, with the space). \"All models\" means both. Do not use \"O3DS\", \"N3DS\", \"original 3DS\", \"3DS XL\" or \"New Nintendo 3DS\" as model labels. Mention the 2DS, 2DS XL or other variants only where they differ in a way that matters, and then name them in the disclaimer.\n- **Disclaimer format.** Inline: end the sentence or bullet with `**New 3DS:** <what differs>.` Block: a blockquote starting `> **New 3DS:**`. In tables with a New 3DS column or row, label it `New 3DS` and keep the Old 3DS column first.\n- **Not a default.** Never write a New 3DS value as the plain statement (\"the CPU runs at 804 MHz\", \"up to 124 MB\"). Write the Old 3DS value, then the disclaimer.\n- **Claims true on both models** may say \"on all models\" once, where a reader might doubt it. Otherwise they stay unmarked, and unmarked means Old 3DS.\n- **Unknown applicability.** If a source does not say which model a fact was checked on, say so with `> Unknown:` instead of assuming Old 3DS.\n- **Evidence and verification.** A `[measured]` result names its model. A code example's verification status lists Old 3DS and New 3DS separately, and an example that uses New 3DS-only features says so up front.\n- **Code.** Examples must work on an Old 3DS. New 3DS-only calls are guarded by a model check and described in a disclaimer.\n- Hardware pages describing a New 3DS-only component (for example the extra CPU cores, the C-Stick or MVD) say so in the first paragraph.\n\n## Evidence labels\n\nEngineering pages, and any performance or behaviour claim elsewhere, must say what supports each non-obvious claim. Tag it inline with one of:\n\n| Label | Meaning |\n| ----- | ------- |\n| `[documented]` | Stated in official documentation or readable in the source code of the library/firmware involved (name the file) |\n| `[reverse-engineered]` | Established through reverse engineering or hardware experiments published by others (name who) |\n| `[measured]` | A benchmark result; give console model, firmware/CFW version, build, and conditions |\n| `[reported]` | A measurement or claim published by a third party that this wiki has not reproduced (developer postmortem, port README, interview, talk). Name the source and its date, the console model, and the conditions as stated; say when the source does not state them. Never present a `[reported]` figure as `[measured]`, and never extend it to other workloads or models |\n| `[hypothesis]` | Plausible but unverified; say what would confirm or refute it |\n\nNever let a `[hypothesis]` or `[reported]` lose its label when it is copied to another page. Advice like \"X is faster\" without a `[measured]` result or a `[documented]` mechanism behind it does not belong in the wiki.\n\nCode examples must state what they were checked against: at minimum, that they compile with a named toolchain/library version. Say explicitly when an example has not been run on hardware.\n\n## Code, benchmarks and verification\n\n- Every code example and benchmark carries a **verification status**: *builds* (with the toolchain versions on the console's source-versions page, no warnings under `-Wall`), *emulator-tested*, *Old 3DS-tested*, *New 3DS-tested*. Record it in the console's source-versions page (CTR: `ctr/engineering/source-versions.md`) and, for benchmarks, in `benchmarks/README.md`. Never upgrade a status without having done the step.\n- Fragments that are not whole programs are compiled inside a minimal `main` with stubs before they are published.\n- Benchmarks live in `<console>/benchmarks/<name>/` as complete projects (Makefile + sources). Their README states the question, the method, the variants to run, and how to record results. Raw results go in the README; the page whose claim they settle gets the `[measured]` label and a link.\n- Emulator timings are never results.\n- When a claim depends on a library or firmware version, pin it: record the commit on the source-versions page and link the source file at that commit when the exact behaviour matters.\n- **When new results arrive, update every page that states the old status.** `tools/check_docs.py` keeps a list of stale status phrases (`STALE_PHRASES`): when a status changes (something is now measured, run, or compared), add the old wording to that list so a page that still repeats it fails the check. `python3 tools/check_docs.py --external` also fetches every external link; CI runs it as an informational job so a citation that stops resolving gets noticed.\n- Emulator checks (`tools/emu_pixel_check.py`, `tools/emu_smoke.py`) are recorded as `emulator-tested` for what they establish (a picture matches, a program finishes) and never as timing; the benchmark README says what each one did and did not exercise.\n- Run `python3 tools/check_docs.py` and `zensical build --strict` (and `tools/build_benchmarks.sh` if code changed) before committing. CI runs all three.\n\n## Writing guidelines\n\n- **Structure every page the same way**: Overview → behavior/fit → Technical details → Homebrew notes (where relevant) → Sources. Readers and agents should always know where the precise facts are.\n- **Define before use.** Never use an acronym or codename without its plain meaning + glossary link on first use per page.\n- **Link aggressively.** At least: first mention of any wiki-covered topic links to its page; first mention of any jargon links to its glossary entry; spec tables link outward rather than duplicating numbers. Use relative links (`../software/os.md`, `../../glossary.md#term` from a `hardware/` or `software/` page).\n- **Cite sources.** Every page ends with Sources. Prefer primary sources (hardware manuals, leaked SDK docs where legally usable, upstream repos, reputable console wikis with verification). Note what each source was used for.\n- **State uncertainty explicitly.** Use `Notes and open questions` or inline `> Unknown:` callouts. Never present a guess as fact. Record the firmware/model/revision a fact was verified against where it matters.\n- **Keep it readable.** Short paragraphs, one idea per paragraph, tables for specs, code blocks or hex tables for layouts. No walls of unexplained hex.\n- **No placeholders.** Don't create a page that is only headings. If research is thin, write the Overview + what is known + open questions, and say so.\n\n## The site (zensical)\n\nThe wiki is published as a static site with [zensical](https://zensical.org/), configured in `zensical.toml`. The site is the wiki: `docs_dir` is the repository root, so every Markdown page in the repository is a wiki page, and the rendered output is written to `site/`.\n\n```bash\npip install zensical\nzensical serve              # live preview on http://localhost:8000/coffeepot/\nzensical build --clean      # write the static site to site/\nzensical build --strict     # same, but fail the build on a broken link or anchor\n```\n\n- **Navigation is explicit.** `nav` in `zensical.toml` lists every page, in the order a reader should meet it. The console `index.md` pages carry the same curated order; keep the two in step.\n- **A new page must be added to `nav`.** A page that is not in `nav` is still built, but it is not reachable from the sidebar.\n- **`exclude_docs` lists what is not a wiki page**: repository plumbing, vendored trees, benchmark build artefacts. Anything added to the repository that is not a page belongs in that list, or it gets published.\n- **Links between pages use source paths** (`../software/os.md`, `../../glossary.md#soc`). zensical rewrites them to site URLs and validates both the target and the anchor, so a broken link fails `zensical build --strict`.\n- `site/` is generated output and is not committed.\n\n## Agent workflow\n\n1. Before writing, search the wiki for existing coverage (`hardware/`, `software/`, `homebrew/`, both glossaries). If a canonical page exists, link to it — don't fork the explanation.\n2. Pick the one correct page type and copy its template. One topic per file, correct directory, kebab-case name.\n3. Draft Overview in plain language first, then fill Technical details completely. If you must choose, include the technical fact with a plain wrapper rather than omitting it.\n4. On first jargon use, add the `**term** ([glossary](path#anchor))` link. If no glossary entry exists, add one in the right glossary (per-device first; promote to global only when the promotion rule above is met).\n5. Cross-link both directions: new page links out to components/formats/tools it depends on; update the console `index.md` hub and any neighbor pages that should point back.               "content": "#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Scratch: read/write PNGs (no PIL here) to crop and scale screenshots.\"\"\"\nimport struct\nimport sys\nimport zlib\n\n\ndef read_png(path):\n    data = open(path, \"rb\").read()\n    assert data[:8] == b\"\\x89PNG\\r\\n\\x1a\\n\", \"not a PNG\"\n    pos = 8\n    idat = bytearray()\n    w = h = depth = color = None\n    while pos + 8 <= len(data):\n        length, kind = struct.unpack(\">I4s\", data[pos:pos + 8])\n        body = data[pos + 8:pos + 8 + length]\n        pos += 12 + length\n        if kind == b\"IHDR\":\n            w, h, depth, color, _c, _f, inter = struct.unpack(\">IIBBBBB\", body)\n            assert depth == 8 and inter == 0, (depth, inter)\n        elif kind == b\"IDAT\":\n            idat += body\n        elif kind == b\"IEND\":\n            break\n    channels = {0: 1, 2: 3, 4: 2, 6: 4}[color]\n    raw = zlib.decompress(bytes(idat))\n    stride = w * channels\n    rows = []\n    prev = bytearray(stride)\n    pos = 0\n    for _ in range(h):\n        kind = raw[pos]\n        line = bytearray(raw[pos + 1:pos + 1 + stride])\n        pos += 1 + stride\n        for i in range(stride):\n            a = line[i - channels] if i >= channels else 0\n            b = prev[i]\n            c = prev[i - channels] if i >= channels else 0\n            if kind == 0:\n                continue\n            if kind == 1:\n                line[i] = (line[i] + a) & 0xFF\n            elif kind == 2:\n                line[i] = (line[i] + b) & 0xFF\n            elif kind == 3:\n                line[i] = (line[i] + ((a + b) >> 1)) & 0xFF\n            elif kind == 4:\n                p = a + b -       "text": "Instructions from: C:\\Users\\terezi\\workdir\\sinjoh\\AGENTS.md\n# AGENTS.md\r\n\r\nRepository-wide rules for agent sessions working on kohjoh.\r\n\r\n## READ THE WIKI \r\n\r\nYou're not expected to have deep technical knowledge of the 3DS platform or how to program efficiently for it. This information has been collected for you already. If it isn't already on disk, clone https://github.com/estyseesghosts/coffeepot.git. Always refer to coffeepot's CTR section when you're writing code or planning project changes - read the relevant hardware, firrmware or engineering articles, so you understand what you're working with. If you can't justify a change with real-hardware evidence or a citation from the wiki, you probably should not do it. Never edit coffeepot yourself. If you notice something genuinely incorrect, PR and tell the user. Always follow the wiki's C style guide.\r\n\r\nThe coffeepot wiki is provided locally on this machine in workdir/coffeepot/.\r\n## Delegating to subagents\r\n\r\nA lead agent must give every subagent it calls **explicit instructions, explicit deliverables and explicit avoidables**. This is not optional, and it matters most for implementer agents: they edit files and cannot rely on chat context the lead has not written down.\r\n\r\nEvery subagent brief must state, in the prompt itself:\r\n\r\n1. **Objective** — the one bounded slice to complete, and why it exists.\r\n2. **Allowed paths** — the exact files or directories the subagent may read and edit.\r\n3. **Deliverables** — the concrete output: code, patch files, tests, docs, and the required report format (files changed, commands run, results, open questions).\r\n4. **Acceptance checks** — the commands or observations that prove the work is done, and the expected result.\r\n5. **Avoidables** — what not to touch or do: paths outside the slice, unrelated refactors, the decomp checkout in place, commits/pushes unless explicitly assigned, and any known traps from `kohjoh.md` or `docs/troubleshooting.md`.\r\n6. **Stopping point** — when to stop and report instead of guessing, for example if the slice grows, the brief conflicts with `kohjoh.md`, or an acceptance check cannot pass.\r\n\r\nDo not send a subagent a vague goal and let it infer scope. If the lead cannot fill in all six items, the slice is not ready to delegate. A brief that is broader, vaguer or in conflict with `kohjoh.md` should be revised before the call, not discovered by the subagent mid-edit.\r\n\r\nImplementer subagents hold `docs/status.md`, `docs/lessons.md` and `kohjoh.md` as required reading; the brief adds the slice-specific detail those files cannot contain. When this file disagrees with an agent definition under `.opencode/agents/` or `.claude/agents/`, this file wins.\r\n\r\n## Git identity\r\n\r\nThe only git identity an agent may use in this repository is:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nterezi <jules@foxtails.me>\r\n```\r\n\r\nSet it in the repository itself before the first commit, and do not rely on a\r\nmachine-wide default or invent a placeholder:\r\n\r\n```sh\r\ngit config user.name terezi\r\ngit config user.email jules@foxtails.me\r\n```\r\n\r\nEvery agent commit carries both fields. Do not use `A4`,\r\n`a4@example.invalid`, the host's auto-detected address, or any other\r\nidentity, and do not author on someone else's behalf. If a commit already\r\nexists under another identity, report it to the lead rather than rewriting\r\nhistory: an artifact's `build-info` names the commit it was built from, and\r\nre-authoring a commit changes that name.\r\n\r\n## Writing Style Rules\r\n\r\nThese rules apply to both chat responses, and to written documentation.\r\n\r\n- **Be direct.** Answer the question immediately. No introductions, filler, or unnecessary conclusions.\r\n- **Use natural language.** Write like a competent engineer, not a marketer, consultant, or chatbot.\r\n- **Be concise, not shallow.** Keep explanations short where possible, but never sacrifice technical detail, accuracy, or important nuance.\r\n- **Avoid AI-sounding prose.** No artificial contrasts, dramatic fragments, forced profundity, rhetorical questions, or rules of three.\r\n- **Don't flatter or validate.** Skip praise, excessive agreement, performative empathy, and conversational pleasantries.\r\n- **Be specific.** Prefer concrete facts, mechanisms, measurements, examples, and actionable steps over vague abstractions.\r\n- **Don't overstructure.** Use headings, lists, and tables only when they genuinely improve readability.\r\n- **Be honest about uncertainty.** Distinguish verified facts, reasonable inferences, and speculation. Don't manufacture confidence.\r\n- **Think critically.** Challenge incorrect assumptions, identify tradeoffs, and explain disagreements without hedging unnecessarily.\r\n- **Prioritize substance.** Every sentence should contribute useful information. If removing it changes nothing, remove it.\r\n\r\n## Truth and Citations \r\n\r\nYou are encouraged to come up with creative solutions for the obscure and arcane problems you might face while working in this folder. This does not mean you just throw shit at the wall to see what sticks.       "text": "Instructions from: C:\\Users\\terezi\\workdir\\coffeepot\\AGENTS.md\n# AGENTS.md — coffeepot\n\nCoffeepot is a wiki for research on Nintendo consoles: their hardware, their software, and homebrew development.\n\nIt serves two readers: a curious human, and a future coding agent doing hardware/software work on these consoles. Every page must work for both.\n\n## Repository layout\n\n```text\nAGENTS.md\nzensical.toml               # site config: navigation, theme, and what is excluded\nglossary.md                  # global jargon glossary\nREADME.md                    # human landing page (what this wiki covers)\n<console>/                   # one directory per console platform (e.g. ctr/, nx/)\n  index.md                   # console overview + hub\n  glossary.md                # per-device jargon glossary\n  hardware/<topic>.md        # one page per hardware component/system\n  software/<topic>.md        # one page per system software / format / service\n  homebrew/<topic>.md        # one page per exploit / tool / library / workflow\n  engineering/<topic>.md     # one page per practical problem (debugging, performance, porting...)\n  benchmarks/<name>/         # buildable benchmark programs + README.md with method and results\ntools/\n  check_docs.py              # link, anchor and Sources-section checker\n  build_benchmarks.sh        # builds every benchmark, fails on warnings\nsite/                        # generated site output (not committed)\n```\n\nCurrent scope is three platforms: `ctr/` (Nintendo 3DS family), `nx/` (Nintendo Switch family) and `oz/` (Nintendo Switch 2 family). Add a new top-level platform directory only for a distinct hardware platform, using its established codename or short kebab-case name (e.g. `ctr`, `nx`, `oz`).\n\nFile names are kebab-case: `arm9-cpu.md`, `nand-filesystem.md`, `boot9strap.md`. One topic per file.\n\n## Core principles\n\n1. **Don't repeat yourself. Link instead.** If something is already explained on another page, summarize it in at most 1–2 sentences and link to the canonical page. Never copy a full explanation into two places.\n2. **Write like a human.** Natural, plain language first. Short paragraphs. Active voice. When jargon is necessary, define it once, link it to a glossary, then use it freely. Never simplify away technical facts (registers, addresses, versions, file offsets, behaviors) to sound readable — push them into a `Technical details` section instead of dropping them.\n4. **Progressive disclosure.** Plain-language summary up top, exhaustive detail below. Human reads the top; agent reads the whole page.\n\n## Jargon and glossaries\n\nJargon means any term a non-expert would stumble on: acronyms (`SoC`, `IPC`), Nintendo-specific codenames (`CTR`, `Horizon`), homebrew terms (`CFW`, `ROP`), and hardware terms used in a precise sense (`physical address`, `kernel privilege`).\n\nRules:\n\n- On first use in a page, give the plain meaning, then the term in bold with a glossary link. Define once here.\n- **Per-device `<console>/glossary.md`**: terms specific to one console (`boot9strap`, `Horizon`, `PICA200`). Define here.\n- If a per-device term starts being used by pages for a second console with the same meaning, promote it to the global glossary and leave a pointer link behind in the per-device glossary.\n- Glossary entries are short: 1–4 sentences of plain meaning, plus the precise technical sense in one more sentence if needed, plus a link to the canonical wiki page for the full story. Never put the full explanation in the glossary; the glossary points at pages, pages point back at the glossary.\n\nGlossary entry format:\n\n```markdown\n<a name=\"anchor-slug\"></a>\n\n### Term name\n\nOne to four sentences: what it is in plain language, then the precise sense. Ends with a link to the canonical page.\n\nExample: <a name=\"soc\"></a>\n\n### System-on-a-chip (SoC)\n```\n\n## Page types\n\nPick exactly one type per page. If a topic spans types (e.g. a chip and its SDK driver), split into linked pages rather than one blended page.\n\n- `<console>/index.md` — console overview and hub. What the console is, when it was sold, what makes it distinctive, spec summary (as a table of links, not raw numbers repeated from subpages), software landscape, homebrew state. Links to every major subpage.\n- `hardware/<topic>.md` — one hardware component or subsystem (CPU, GPU, memory map, display, input, cartridge, wireless). What it does, where it sits in the system, its observable behavior, then full specs.\n- `software/<topic>.md` — one software thing (OS/kernel, system menu, applet, file format, filesystem, system service, update mechanism). What the user sees, what a developer needs to know, formats and behaviors.\n- `homebrew/<topic>.md` — one exploit, custom firmware, tool, library, or workflow. What it achieves, who it is for, how it works, how to use it, limits and risks.\n- `engineering/<topic>.md` — one practical problem a developer faces when writing software for the console (debugging, profiling, performance, memory management, rendering, asset conversion, hardware testing). They link to the reference pages for facts rather than restating them.\n\n## Templates\n\nCopy the matching template. Use tables for registers/specs. Do not simplify here. In tables with a New 3DS column or row, label it `New 3DS` and keep the Old 3DS column first.\n- **Not a default.** Never write a New 3DS value as the plain statement (\"the CPU runs at 804 MHz\", \"up to 124 MB\"). Write the Old 3DS value, then the disclaimer.\n- **Claims true on both models** may say \"on all models\" once, where a reader might doubt it. Tag it inline with one of:\n\n| Label | Meaning |\n| ----- | ------- |\n| `[documented]` | Stated in official documentation or readable in the source code of the library/firmware involved (name the file) |\n| `[reverse-engineered]` | Established through reverse engineering or hardware experiments published by others (name who) |\n| `[measured]` | A benchmark result; give console model, firmware/CFW version, build, and conditions |\n| `[reported]` | A measurement or claim published by a third party that this wiki has not reproduced (developer postmortem, port README, interview, talk). Never present a `[reported]` figure as `[measured]`, and never extend it to other workloads or models |\n| `[hypothesis]` | Plausible but unverified; say what would confirm or refute it |\n\nNever let a `[hypothesis]` or `[reported]` lose its label when it is copied to another page.
