Raw results go in the README; the page whose claim they settle gets the `[measured]` label and a link.\n- Emulator timings are never results.\n- When a claim depends on a library or firmware version, pin it: record the commit on the source-versions page and link the source file at that commit when the exact behaviour matters.\n- **When new results arrive, update every page that states the old status.** `tools/check_docs.py` keeps a list of stale status phrases (`STALE_PHRASES`): when a status changes (something is now measured, run, or compared), add the old wording to that list so a page that still repeats it fails the check. `python3 tools/check_docs.py --external` also fetches every external link; CI runs it as an informational job so a citation that stops resolving gets noticed.\n- Emulator checks (`tools/emu_pixel_check.py`, `tools/emu_smoke.py`) are recorded as `emulator-tested` for what they establish (a picture matches, a program finishes) and never as timing; the benchmark README says what each one did and did not exercise.\n- Run `python3 tools/check_docs.py` and `zensical build --strict` (and `tools/build_benchmarks.sh` if code changed) before committing. A pixel that was the game's own moved along (the\r\n217: opening's Pokémon, moved so that they come in from the wide screen's edge;\r\n218: the map's beyond the DS's edge copied into a band; a strip of sprites\r\n219: copied on) is a marker that says how far (red and blue, green: see\r\n220: `nitro_port_wideart.h`), and the port draws the game's pixel from that far\r\n221: back. A picture of a layer the port lays out in parts is shared only\r\n237: where it was made (its layout's place). So:\r\n238: \r\n239: 1. Copy `DIR/share/*.png` into the repository's `wideart/` folder, and the\r\n250:    layouts' pictures (`party_panel.png`, `pc_boxes_divider.png`...: drawn\r\n251:    whole by hand, so as they are) from `wide/` too. A picture shared with\r\n252:    nothing left in it (`0 yours`, no pixel of the game's moved: a layer\r\n253:    captured and saved as it was) adds nothing; leave it out. A picture of\r\n254:    a text window (a message box, a shop's list of names) changes its key\r\n255:    with the text and what the game put where, and is the game's text: leave\r\n256:    it out too.\r\n257: 3. GPUREG_SH_OPDESCS_DATAi\n\n\n\n\n\nOverview\nGPU internal registers are written to through GPU commands. They are used to control the GPU's behavior, that is to say tell it to draw stuff and how we want it drawn.\nEach command is at least 8 bytes wide. The first word is the command parameter and the second word constitutes the command header. Optionally, more parameter words may follow (potentially including a padding word to align commands to multiples of 8 bytes).\nIn the simplest case, a command is exactly 8 bytes wide. You can think of such a command as writing the parameter word to an internal register (the index of which is given in the command header). The more general case where more than one parameter word is given is equivalent to multiple simple commands (one for each parameter word). If consecutive writing mode is enabled in the command header, the current command index will be incremented after each parameter write. Otherwise, the parameters will be consecutively written to the same register.\nFor example, the sequence \"0xAAAAAAAA 0x802F011C 0xBBBBBBBB 0xCCCCCCCC\" is equivalent to a call to commands 0xF011C with parameter 0xAAAAAAAA, 0xF011D with parameter 0xBBBBBBBB and 0xF011E with parameter 0xCCCCCCCC. If consecutive writing mode were disabled, the command would be equivalent to three consecutive calls to 0xF011C (once with parameter 0xAAAAAAAA, once with 0xBBBBBBBB, and finally with 0xCCCCCCCC).\nInvalid GPU command parameters including NaN floats can cause the GPU to hang, which then causes the GSP module to hang as well.\nThe size of GPU command buffers must be 0x10-byte aligned; the lower 3 bits of the size are cleared. A common pitfall is having the finalization command (write to register 0x0010) not executed because it was the last 8 bytes of a non-0x10 byte aligned command buffer, and having the GPU hang as a result.\n\nCommand Header\n\n\nBit\n\nDescription\n\n\n0-15\n\nCommand ID\n\n\n16-19\n\nParameter mask\n\n\n20-27\n\nNumber of extra parameters (may be zero)\n\n\n28-30\n\nUnused\n\n\n31\n\nConsecutive writing mode\n\nParameter masking\nUsing a value other than 0xF, parts of a word in internal GPU memory can be updated without touching the other bits of it. For example, setting bit 16 to zero indicates that the least significant byte of the parameter will not be overwritten, setting bit 17 to zero indicates that the parameter's second LSB will not be overwritten, etc. This means that for instance commands 0x00010107 and 0x00020107 refer to the same thing but write different parts of the parameter.\n\nTypes\nThere are three main types of registers :\n\nconfiguration registers, which directly map to various rendering properties (for example: GPUREG_FACECULLING_CONFIG)\ndata transfer registers, which can be seen as FIFOs that let us send sequential chunks of data to the GPU, such as shader code or 1D samplers (for example: GPUREG_GSH_CODETRANSFER_DATA)\naction triggering registers, which tell the GPU to do something, like draw a primitive (for example: GPUREG_DRAWARRAYS)\nAliases\nIt is possible for multiple register (sequential) IDs to correspond to the same register. This is done to leverage the consecutive writing mode for GPU commands, which makes it possible for a single command to write data to multiple sequential register IDs. For example, register IDs 02C1 through 02C8 all correspond to GPUREG_VSH_FLOATUNIFORM_DATAi so that a consecutively writing command based at 02C0 will write its first parameter to GPUREG_VSH_FLOATUNIFORM_INDEX and ever subsequent ones to GPUREG_VSH_FLOATUNIFORM_DATAi\n\nData Types\n\n\nName\n\nDescription\n\n\nsigned\n\nSigned integer\n\n\nunsigned\n\nUnsigned integer\n\n\nfloatX.Y.Z\n\nFloating-point number with X sign bits, Y exponent bits, and Z mantissa bits\n\n\nfixedX.Y.Z\n\nFixed-point number with X sign bits, Y integer bits, and Z fractional My last build added a temporary diagnostic (a debug quad showing the wide-art texture across the whole canvas, plus a log of the texture's texels) to bisect \"the texture never reaches the GPU\" from \"the draw state/geometry is wrong\". That build's flag didn't take (`WIDEART_DEBUG` didn't reach the compile), so the run produced no diagnostic output; I'm checking the make expansion now.\n\n## What has gone well\n\n- **The art key is bit-exact with pokeplatinum-3ds.** Two live layer keys during the intro came out as `c348e56dbb30d48a` and `6d5a3d55615351bf` — exactly the names of two built-in pictures. That was the load-bearing unknown: the pictures are *named* by that hash, so any mismatch meant the pictures were never found.\n- **The package-time precompute is verified.** `pack_wideart.py` produces a blob whose texture content I compared pixel-for-pixel against the source PNGs for all 24 pictures: **0 mismatches** (including the PICA Morton/tile layout, which I cross-checked against kohjoh's `swz()` and coffeepot's tex3ds-verified layout, and against the atlas's own conversion in this engine).\n- **The runtime plumbing works**: blob parse, texture allocation, lookup by key with p3ds's wrapped-distance rule, band quad geometry checked against p3ds's `SEG_ART` model (the picture's content sits at canvas x + dx; the bands show the picture's edges and nothing else).\n- **Two real bugs found and fixed**: the blob header was 18 bytes against the reader's 16 (misaligned table → nothing matched), and citro3d's `checkTexSize` refuses a 512×576 texture (now 512×1024 with only the 576 rows the bands use in the blob).\n- **A measurement error of my own, worth recording**: I had been judging \"the bands are black\" from a screenshot taken at t=40 s — the name-entry screen, which has no wide art at all. The harness's `-Shots` are *seconds*, not frames. The band quads are in fact created (the log says `engine 1 (top) bg 3 band key 6d5a3d55615351bf scrolled 0`).\n\n## What has gone poorly\n\n- **`tools/build.ps1` is still broken** (its `export PATH='...:$PATH'` sets a literal `$PATH`; `-Clean` throws a `SwitchParameter` error). I've been building through a direct MSYS2 invocation instead.\n- **Two wasted cycles on diagnostics that were never wired up**: `log_band()` was written but never called, and the `WIDEART_DEBUG` define didn't reach the compile, so a run I was counting on produced nothing.\n- **Log noise**: `log_art_key` re-logged every frame for keys that have a picture (612 lines in one run). Fixed to log once per key.\n\n## Where the fault most likely is\n\nThree candidates, in order: the **PICA's handling of a 512×1024 texture** (the atlas is 1024×1024, so it has never exercised a tall texture — the `TEXUNITi_DIM` register holds height in bits 0-10 and width in bits 16-26, and citro3d's `dim` union fills them the other way round in this shape); the **upload** (1 MiB in the linear heap, `C3D_TexFlush` after the copy); or the **draw state** (scissor widened to the full target, texture rebound to unit 0, uvscale reset to the atlas afterwards — each bind costs a texture-cache clear, which is also a cost I have to fix for the Old 3DS budget).\n\nOnce the bands show, the remaining wide-art work is the two documented gaps: the picture's middle is not drawn (the layer's own tiles are there instead — equivalent for the built-in pictures, whose middles are all markers), and the game's own pixels *beyond* the DS's edge are not composited into the band (deferred: p3ds does that in software, which is the path we're not taking). Then I'll commit this milestone and move to the lower-screen field menu."
